historical_timeline.summary: Smallpox at Hampton Court, with recovery.
A visitor describes her teeth as black.
The Earl of Essex is executed.
An ache in her arm, side, and hip; otherwise in good health through the summer.
Strains her foot and falls entering her barge; low spirits and little appetite in her godson's letter.
A cold before the move to Richmond; well amended there.
Her cousin and lady of the Privy Chamber, the Countess of Nottingham, dies; the Queen grieves.
Sleeplessness, poor appetite, deep melancholy, refusal of food, rest, and physic; her chaplain dates her melancholy by fits to the previous three or four months.

historical_timeline.summary: Dies at Richmond Palace, aged 69; causes proposed later are disputed.

claims.statement: Elizabeth was born at Greenwich on 7 September 1533 (Julian calendar; 17 September 1533 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar), the daughter of Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn.
Her mother, Anne Boleyn, was executed in 1536, when Elizabeth was two; her father, Henry VIII, reigned until 1547.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; the cause of her father's death is not recorded in the cited source.

claims.statement: She succeeded her half-sister Mary I on Mary's death in November 1558 and never married.

In October 1562, aged 29, she fell ill at Hampton Court with a fever that turned to smallpox. On 15 October she wrote that a hot fever prevented her writing more; the Spanish ambassador reported that she lost her speech and was thought lost, that the eruption appeared in the night, and that she then improved. The court feared for the succession, and she recovered.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Dates in the source are Julian; the illness ran in the second half of October 1562.

claims.statement: Lady Sidney, who nursed her through the smallpox, caught it and was scarred for life; the court chronology states that, unlike the Queen, she was scarred. A medal struck for the Queen's recovery shows her face unblemished.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The roster's lead of facial scarring from smallpox is not supported by this source.

claims.statement: A German visitor who saw her at Greenwich in August 1598, in her 65th year, described her face as fair but wrinkled and her teeth as black, a defect he attributed to the English use of sugar.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An eyewitness description; it says nothing of the cause.

claims.statement: A museum account of her death states that she had lost most of her teeth and her hair by the end of her life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A summary statement by a national museum; no contemporary witness is quoted for it.

claims.statement: On 25 February 1601 (Julian) the Earl of Essex, once her favourite, was executed at the Tower after his rising.
Through 1602 court letters describe an ache in her arm that later spread to her side and hip; in September observers wrote that her health was very good and that she hunted and rode often.
In December 1602 (Julian) she strained her foot leaving a dinner at her secretary's new house and, refusing help, stumbled and fell entering her barge, bruising her shins, which soon healed.

On 27 December 1602 (Julian), her godson Sir John Harington wrote that she now bore show of human infirmity: he had found her in a most pitiable state, she wept at the memory of the Irish war in which he had served with the Earl of Essex, she said she was past her relish for his verses, and she told him that her bodily meat did not suit her and that she had eaten only one ill-tasted cake since the night before.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A contemporary letter; it records low spirits and poor appetite but no diagnosis.

claims.statement: In January 1603 (Julian) she caught a cold shortly before the court moved from Whitehall to Richmond on 21 January, and was reported well amended of it at Richmond. On 6 February she received the Venetian envoy in state and spoke at length.

The Countess of Nottingham, her cousin and a lady of her Privy Chamber since 1559, died on 25 February 1603 (Julian). The French ambassador wrote that the Queen asked to be excused audiences while she got over her grief and had shed many tears for her.

In March 1603 (Julian) her secretary wrote that for eight or nine days she had been much deprived of sleep, which decayed her appetite; another observer wrote that she rested ill at night and abstained more than usual from her meat; and a third that for some twenty days she had slept very little and her sleep and stomach had left her.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary letters; sleeplessness and poor appetite are recorded, not diagnosed.

claims.statement: Her cousin Robert Carey, who reached Richmond in March 1603, wrote that she told him her heart had been sad and heavy for ten or twelve days, sighed forty or fifty times as they spoke, and that her melancholy was too deep-rooted to be removed; she then sat on cushions for at least four days and nights and could not be persuaded to eat or to go to bed, and refused all remedies.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An eyewitness memoir written in the 1620s.

claims.statement: The French ambassador reported in March 1603 that she had said she wished not to live any longer but desired to die, that she took no medicine, and that everyone agreed melancholy was the true cause of her illness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A diplomat's report of her words; it is recorded here without interpretation.

claims.statement: On 23 March 1603 (Julian) a royal chaplain told the diarist John Manningham that she had been troubled with melancholy by fits for some three or four months and for the last fortnight had been extremely oppressed by it, refusing to eat, to take physic, or to rest in bed; that she had always kept her senses and memory; and that her physicians thought she had a firm constitution likely to have lived many years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The chaplain's account dates the onset of her low spirits to late 1602.

claims.statement: Another letter of March 1603 reported that she complained of an imposthumation in her head, aches in her bones, and continual cold in her legs, with a notable decay of judgement and memory; William Camden wrote of her sleepless indisposition joined with an inflammation from the breast upward.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The report of failing memory conflicts with the chaplain's statement that she kept her senses and memory (CLM-0017).

claims.statement: She died at Richmond Palace between one and two in the morning of 24 March 1603 (Julian; 3 April 1603 Gregorian), aged 69, after growing speechless the day before; by English legal reckoning, in which the year began on 25 March, the date was written as 1602.
A museum account links her late bouts of melancholy to the deaths of her long-serving lady-in-waiting and of the Earl of Essex.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A later interpretation of her grief.

claims.statement: Proposed causes of her death include blood poisoning from a lead-based white face paint (Venetian ceruse), pneumonia, a streptococcal infection of the tonsils, and cancer; no post-mortem was allowed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective suggestions only; none is established, and lead poisoning is not used in the modern episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate and treat major depression in a 69-year-old woman who holds a demanding lifelong public office, after several bereavements, following the 2019 APA depression guideline (combined second-generation antidepressant and interpersonal psychotherapy for older adults), the 2022 VA/DoD MDD guideline, the CMID depression monograph, and the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria: a presenting problem of low mood, poor sleep, poor intake, and weight loss worked up for medical causes (blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, albumin, thyroid, vitamin B12, folate, a cognitive screen, and a medication review that stops an anticholinergic sleep aid); PHQ-9 and GDS-15 for measurement-based care; suicide-risk assessment with a passive death wish, a safety plan, and the 988 Lifeline, reviewed at every visit; sertraline started low and raised slowly, with a sodium check for SSRI-related hyponatremia; CBT for insomnia rather than hypnotics; nutrition, dental care, and weight; falls prevention while starting an SSRI; grief distinguished from depression; and the privacy of a public figure.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Tudor returns two weeks after her first visit. She stopped the over-the-counter diphenhydramine that night; for three nights she slept worse, and she now sleeps about four hours, waking at 2 or 3 in the morning and lying awake with thoughts of the friends she has lost. She has kept the sleep diary and the fixed rising time and has stopped napping after dinner. Her appetite is still poor; she takes the nutrition supplement once a day and has lost a further 0.3 kg. She still postpones audiences and has not played music or ridden. She has not had the wish not to wake since the first visit and has no thoughts of harming herself; she keeps her safety plan in her desk. She saw Dr. Rasmussen-Hale of geriatric psychiatry this afternoon. She came at the end of the day, as arranged, and asks again that nothing about her care leave the clinic.

assessment_plan.assessment: Three months of pervasive low mood, loss of interest, early waking, poor appetite with weight loss, slowed thinking, guilt, and a passive death wish, with PHQ-9 17 then 16 and GDS-15 10. Hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, MCV 92 fL, sodium 139 mmol/L, creatinine 0.74 mg/dL, glucose 88 mg/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, vitamin B12 410 pg/mL, and folate 9.8 ng/mL are normal, and the MoCA was 27, so no medical cause or cognitive disorder is found. Grief is part of the picture, but its pervasiveness, the weight loss, and the death wish point to a major depressive episode. Dr. Rasmussen-Hale confirms the diagnosis, with no bipolar or psychotic features. The passive death wish has not recurred
plan: Sertraline 25 mg each morning for one week, then 50 mg if she has no side effects; review in about four weeks, sooner by telephone if needed
Weekly individual interpersonal psychotherapy with the clinic psychologist, in private end-of-day sessions, focused on grief

hpi.narrative: Ms. Tudor is a 69-year-old woman treated for major depression, one week after starting sertraline 25 mg, who came in the same day with a sore throat for two days. It began with a runny nose and sneezing after several of her staff had colds, and she now has a dry cough, a hoarse voice, and pain on swallowing. Her temperature at home was 37.8 C last night. She can swallow liquids and soft food, though she has eaten even less than usual, and she is drinking about a liter a day. She has no trouble opening her mouth, no drooling, no difficulty breathing, no ear pain, no rash, and no neck stiffness. She has taken no throat lozenges or cold remedies, remembering the advice about over-the-counter night-time products. She has had no nausea, diarrhea, headache, restlessness, or bleeding on sertraline. Her mood is unchanged; she has had no thoughts of death or of harming herself since the first visit.

referral.question: Low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite, and 6 percent weight loss over three months in a 69-year-old woman after several bereavements, with PHQ-9 17, GDS-15 10, and a passive death wish. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on treatment suited to an older adult and on her safety
referral.urgency: Soon, within two weeks; passive death wish without intent or plan, with a safety plan in place
referral.pertinent_history: Ms. Tudor is a 69-year-old woman who has held a lifelong public office as head of state for more than forty years. Over three months she has had heavy low mood, loss of interest in music and riding, waking at 2 or 3 in the morning with about four hours of sleep, poor appetite, and a fall in weight from 55.9 to 52.4 kg (height 163 cm). Over the past two years several of those closest to her have died, including a former protégé and confidant after a bitter breach, and two friends of her own generation. On some mornings she wishes she would not wake; she has no active thoughts, intent, plan, or past self-harm, there are no firearms in her residence, and her maid keeps her medicines. A collaborative safety plan with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was made today. PHQ-9 17 (item 9 scored 1), GDS-15 10, MoCA 27. She has been taking over-the-counter diphenhydramine for sleep for six weeks; it was stopped today. Her upper partial denture is loose and chewing is painful. She stumbled and fell boarding a boat three weeks ago, bruising her shins. Blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, albumin, TSH, vitamin B12, and folate were sent today. She is very concerned about privacy and asks that her care stay within the clinic
questions: Do you confirm a major depressive episode, as distinct from grief, and are there bipolar, psychotic, or cognitive features?
Which antidepressant, starting dose, and titration do you advise at 69, with low weight and a recent fall?
Which psychotherapy do you recommend, given her bereavements and her need for privacy?
Do you agree with the suicide-risk assessment and the safety plan?
How should her insomnia be treated now that diphenhydramine has stopped?
How long should treatment continue, and what would make you want to see her again?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Tudor is seen at the request of Dr. Ashcombe-Nwosu, two weeks after her first visit, at the end of the clinic day at her request. She describes three months of a heavy, unremitting low mood that does not lift with good news, loss of pleasure in music, riding, and company, waking at 2 or 3 in the morning, poor appetite with weight loss, slowed thinking, and a sense that she has outlived her circle. She dwells on a former protégé and confidant who died two years ago after a bitter breach, and on her own part in it, with guilt that comes in waves. She has had no period of elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, or racing thoughts, and no hallucinations or fixed false beliefs. The passive wish not to wake has not recurred since the first visit; she has never harmed herself. She has no memory complaints and continues to manage her papers. She stopped diphenhydramine two weeks ago and sleeps about four hours. She drinks a small glass of wine some evenings. She prefers to be treated privately and individually and is willing to take a medicine if it is explained to her

No bipolar or psychotic features; no evidence of a neurocognitive disorder; normal tests exclude common medical causes.
